summary: Presents a mechanism based on threads that prevents MPLS from setting up label switched paths that contain loops. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A thread tied to a runner would tangle if the runner went in circles. This idea uses a tracing thread to spot paths that loop back.

questions: how to avoid loops in label switched paths
what is a thread color in mpls
what does rewinding a thread mean
subtitle: A thread-based way for MPLS routers to confirm a path has no loop before handing out labels.

tldr.problem: When routes change, MPLS could set up label switched paths (LSPs) that contain loops.
tldr.mechanism: A router that gets a new next hop sends a uniquely colored thread downstream. If the thread comes back to a router it already passed, there is a loop. If not, the thread is rewound upstream and labels are assigned only as it rewinds.
tldr.outcome: The state carried in messages is fixed in size, and only nodes downstream of a change take part. The memo is Experimental.

today: RFC 3063 is an Experimental RFC from February 2001, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Threads Against Loops
sections.content:
RFC 3063 presents a mechanism based on threads that prevents MPLS from setting up label switched paths with loops. When a label switching router (LSR) finds a new next hop for a forwarding equivalence class (FEC), it creates a thread and extends it downstream. Each thread gets a unique color.

If there is a loop, some thread arrives back at an LSR it has already passed, and the color reveals it. When no loop is found, threads are rewound to the point of creation, and labels are assigned as they rewind. Labels are not assigned until loop freedom is guaranteed.

The mechanism works whether some, all or none of the LSRs support VC merge, and with ordered downstream-on-demand or ordered downstream allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: Before giving out street signs, a scout walks the route with a colored string. If the scout runs into their own string, the route goes in a circle.

sections.title: Link Hop Counts and Next Hop Events
sections.content:
An LSP is treated as a multipoint-to-point tree rooted at the egress node. Each link has a link hop count: the number of hops between the link and the furthest upstream leaf node. The downstream link's count is one more than the largest incoming count, a quantity called Hmax.

The RFC defines three events: next hop acquisition, next hop loss, and next hop change. A change is handled as a loss on the old next hop followed by an acquisition on the new one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each road segment is numbered by how many steps it is from the farthest starting point. A new road costs one more step than the longest road leading into it.

sections.title: Thread Attributes
sections.content:
A thread has three attributes, which may be encoded in one thread object: a color, a hop count and a TTL. The color is unique in time and space: an IP address of the node joined with an event identifier from a numbering space the node maintains. The color value of all zeros is reserved as transparent.

The hop count is carried in path control messages. A special value unknown (0xff) is used when a loop is found and is not increased as the thread extends. The TTL is decremented at each hop, and a message with TTL zero is not forwarded, which avoids infinite looping of control messages.

A thread forms a loop if the same colored thread arrives on multiple incoming links, or if the color was assigned by the receiving node.
sections.plainLanguage: Each scout carries a name tag nobody else has, a step counter, and a countdown so they eventually give up.

sections.title: The Five Thread Actions
sections.content:
Five primitive actions make up the algorithm. Extending sends a path setup message downstream. Merging folds a new thread into an existing outgoing thread without sending messages, when it forms no loop and the outgoing link hop count is at least one greater. Stalling stores a looping thread's color and hop count on the receiving link without extending it.

Rewinding returns an acknowledgment upstream when a colored thread reaches the egress node, or reaches a node whose outgoing link is transparent with a high enough hop count. Rewound links become transparent, and a node can start label switching once all its links are transparent. Withdrawing tears down the path downstream of a node after a next hop change or loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The scout can pass the string on, join an existing string, stop at a tangle, report back that the way is clear, or pull the string back in.

sections.title: The Algorithm and Where It Applies
sections.content:
A node that acquires a next hop creates a colored thread and extends it. A received colored thread is stalled, merged, rewound or extended, and a thread with TTL zero is never extended. When a thread is stalled and the node has no unstalled incoming links and is not an eligible leaf node, it withdraws. Otherwise, a thread of unknown hop count may be created and extended.

The same algorithm supports loop prevention and loop detection. In prevention mode, a label mapping is sent only on rewind. In detection mode, a node returns a label mapping without a thread object right after receiving a colored thread. It can also keep using the old path while the new one loops, adapt to ordered downstream allocation, and support load splitting by giving separate LSPs different colors.
sections.plainLanguage: The same scout trick can either stop a bad road from being built or just warn you that one exists, and it can keep the old road open meanwhile.

sections.title: Comparison and Security
sections.content:
The RFC compares threads with the path-vector/diffusion method. Thread sizes are constant, while a path-vector grows with the LSP length. A node changing its next hop interacts only with nodes between it and the egress on the new path, so misbehaving nodes off the path cannot delay setup. Threads suit both allocation modes, are described as retry-free, and allow the old path to be used if there is a layer 3 loop on the new one.

The Security Considerations section says the procedures have no security impact beyond that generally present in the use of any MPLS procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Other methods make the scout carry a longer and longer list of places visited. This one carries a single tag, so it stays light however far the trip goes.

items.label: Extending
items.desc: Send a path setup message downstream, with or without changing color.

items.label: Merging
items.desc: Fold a new thread into an existing outgoing thread; no message sent.

items.label: Stalling
items.desc: Store a looping thread on the link without extending it.

items.label: Rewinding
items.desc: Acknowledge upstream once loop freedom is established; links become transparent.

items.label: Withdrawing
items.desc: Tear down the path downstream after a next hop change or loss.

fields.name: Color
fields.desc: Node IP address plus event identifier; all zeros is transparent.

fields.name: Hop Count
fields.desc: Hops from the furthest upstream leaf; 0xff means unknown.

fields.name: TTL
fields.desc: Decremented at each hop; at 0 the message is not forwarded.
